title: How Seed Banks Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore seed banks: why they exist (an ancient practice, crop diversity, war, climate change, medicinal plant research), the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway as the most famous example, how seeds are collected, cleaned, dried, and stored in cold storage, the orthodox vs. recalcitrant seed distinction, periodic regrowing and genetic testing, the debate between seed banking and in-field farmer support, the Kew Millennium Seed Bank, the Vavilov Institute in St. Petersburg, and a myth that Svalbard was flooded by climate change. The episode also includes tour announcements, off-topic banter, and listener mail about the Aurora borealis.
topics: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts announce 2017 North America tour dates and chat about favorite seeds, a crock pot recipe, and long-form journalism.

segments.title: Introduction to seed banks and Svalbard
segments.summary: Introduction to the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway as the most famous seed bank, and Debbie Ronka's article. Seed banking is an ancient practice, dating to Mesopotamia about 7,750 years ago.

segments.title: Why seed banks matter: crop diversity
segments.summary: Crop diversity is key. The Irish potato famine showed the danger of uniform crops, and Norman Borlaug's green revolution led to homogenized varieties, which made the 1970s US corn blight severe, cutting yields by a quarter to half.

segments.title: Reasons to bank seeds: climate, war, medicine
segments.summary: Reasons for seed banks include climate change, natural and man-made disasters such as war (which has looted Middle Eastern seed banks and displaced farmers), and future medical research, since many wild plants are used for medicine.

segments.title: Seed bank operators and the Global Crop Diversity Trust
segments.summary: There are about 1,400 seed banks worldwide. The Global Crop Diversity Trust and the Svalbard vault serve as a backup repository; depositors alone can withdraw seeds. The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources was ratified in 2004 by 40 governments. Concerns exist about big agriculture and standard-setting.
topics: International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources

segments.title: Collecting, cleaning, drying, and storing seeds
segments.summary: Process: decide what to collect, collect when ripe, record soil and ecosystem data, assign sample numbers, clean and dry seeds to about 15 percent relative humidity, and store at about negative 18 C. Orthodox seeds can be stored this way; recalcitrant seeds cannot, and cryopreservation is used for some plants such as bananas.

segments.title: Seed management, regrowing, and the debate over banking vs. farmers
segments.summary: Stored seeds must be periodically regrown and rebanked, and genetic info should be catalogued. Critics argue seeds may become less useful over time and that halting evolution is a problem. The debate pits seed banking against in-field support for farmers, with funding limits.

segments.title: Other seed banks and Svalbard flooding myth
segments.summary: Other seed banks include the Millennium Seed Bank at Kew in London and the Vavilov Institute in St. Petersburg, where scientists starved during the Leningrad siege. Media reports of Svalbard flooding due to permafrost melt were overblown; the vault was built into permafrost, not flooded by climate change.

segments.title: Listener mail: Northern lights
segments.summary: Listener Maya Yurick from Minneapolis describes seeing the Aurora borealis at a music festival, pushing back on an earlier episode that suggested the lights are disappointing.
